Al- though the second rule sounds even more obvious than the first one, in this case the gap between intentions and effects might also be quite wide. One example is the kind of argumentation based on de-generalising: “peo - ple shall not blame all migrants for the terrorist attacks, since migrants come from so many different countries that it is useless to put them all in a box” . While apparently useful in the short term, this counter argument does not hit the psychological scapegoating mechanism at the basis of the narrative and its most common result is to specify the target of hate better (and with reinforced argumentations): “if it is not all migrants, it is for sure the Muslim migrants” . Al- though the second rule sounds even more obvious than the first one, in this case the gap between intentions and effects might also be quite wide. One example is the kind of argumentation based on de-generalising: “peo - ple shall not blame all migrants for the terrorist attacks, since migrants come from so many different countries that it is useless to put them all in a box” . While apparently useful in the short term, this counter argument does not hit the psychological scapegoating mechanism at the basis of the narrative and its most common result is to specify the target of hate better (and with reinforced argumentations): “if it is not all migrants, it is for sure the Muslim migrants” . These “paths of hate” were observed especially after the terrorist attacks in European countries in 2015 and 2016, with hate speech concentrat- ing on Muslim and male migrants (or perceived as such). CHAPTER 5 | COUNTER AND ALTERNATIVE NAR RATIVES Human rights campaigners should be aware that counter arguments ad- dressing the effects of hate, especially those focusing on diverting the at - tention from a specific target, do not challenge the underlying causes and the negative emotions at the basis, hate and fear. If negative emotions are not addressed, the “pattern of hate” will simply repeat itself targeting a dif- ferent group.
